analysis.title: Perspectives – Financial Markets, November/December 2026
key_insights: US Treasury yields fell in October on weak labour market data and worries about AI overinvestment. USD credit spreads widened, with CCC spreads underperforming most.
Swiss Life expects the Fed to deliver two additional rate hikes because US inflation stays above target amid a resilient labour market. The 10-year US yield is 4.9%, down 35 bps in October.

TMT credit spreads widened in October on higher rates and elevated bond supply, raising spread volatility across AI infrastructure credit (AI cloud providers, firms linked to leading AI developers, BBB/BB data centre project finance bonds). The AI capex versus AI revenue and circular financing debate intensified.

An unwinding of the AI trade would support government bonds, since lower AI capex implies weaker data centre construction, reduced corporate borrowing, softer commodity demand and a smaller growth and inflation impulse.

Swiss Life is neutral on USD IG and HY spreads, positive on EUR IG (it sees the widening in French sovereign and EUR IG spreads as overdone), and neutral on 2-year and 10-year government bond yields in the US, eurozone and Switzerland over a 1-month horizon.

The ECB held rates in October. Swiss Life expects one more hike, likely in December 2026, then a hold. That is less tightening than the market priced, though market expectations moved toward Swiss Life's view in October.
UK core inflation rose to 2.8% in September. The autumn budget was viewed as solid and lowered 10-year Gilt yields. Swiss Life expects two more Bank of England hikes.
Swiss Life expects the SNB to hike twice by 25 bps in 2027, citing the relatively weak CHF and improved economic data.

Q3 earnings season is about halfway through with strong results. Consensus earnings growth is 27% in the US (median company 8-9%), 72% in emerging markets, 22% in Europe and 11% in Switzerland. Upward revisions outnumber downward ones.

Earnings growth is highly concentrated. In the US, IT and energy are expected to generate about 80% of growth, and Micron and Nvidia alone account for 35%. In EM, 90% comes from North Asia and over 80% from IT. In Europe, energy and financials supply about 70%.

Swiss Life sees a broad-based equity correction as unlikely and does not expect an imminent unwind of the AI trade. The real test comes when data centre capacity becomes operational and depreciation, write-downs and leasing costs show up. It sees modest equity upside from stable rates and Q4 seasonality.
October equity performance (MSCI, local currency): US +0.9% (YTD +13.3%), Eurozone -0.5% (+10.3%), UK +1.3% (+11.0%), Switzerland +6.4% (+13.6%), EM -6.5% (+15.3%).

EUR was the worst major currency in October, down about 2% trade-weighted, on French political and fiscal concerns and ECB uncertainty. ECB President Lagarde's departure announcement at month end added to the uncertainty.

Swiss Life moved to neutral on EUR/USD (now near fair value by 5-year real yield differentials) and EUR/CHF (from negative). It still expects USD appreciation against most majors except EUR, and expects GBP to weaken against EUR and USD in November after a 1.5% trade-weighted rise.
The BoJ is expected to hike in December. Swiss Life views the pace as too slow to remove JPY depreciation pressure against USD.

Asset allocation: overweight global equities (October's correction seen as a healthy reality check), neutral government bonds with a preference for shorter duration, underweight investment-grade credit. Within equities it favours US, EM and European (Germany) equities.

The report points to the MOVE Index (Treasury volatility) as a complement to the VIX, noting that rate volatility can hit portfolios through discount rates, financing conditions and correlations even when equity volatility is contained.

sector_views.rationale: No imminent AI trade unwind expected, but earnings growth is concentrated in IT (Micron and Nvidia are 35% of US growth), and AI credit exposure is rotating out on valuation and rate sensitivity.
Favours Swiss NAV-based real estate and infrastructure, and is tactically increasing exposure to Swiss traded real estate.
Together they account for about 70% of expected European earnings growth.

Depreciation, write-downs and capacity leasing costs once data centre capacity becomes operational.

tension_points.bull_case: Earnings growth is exceptionally strong, upward revisions outnumber downward ones, and the reassessment of AI investment reflects a healthier balance. No imminent unwind is expected.
tension_points.bear_case: Concentrated earnings growth, elevated AI valuations that leave little room for misses, circular financing and AI credit spread widening could trigger a rotation out of AI exposure and support government bonds.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Depreciation charges, potential write-downs and capacity leasing costs showing up once current data centre and computing investments become operational.
